record.paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
record.context_brief: Massive black holes in spiral hosts
record.original_question: If corrected estimates place black-hole masses in radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies as high as 10^8–10^9 solar masses, including about 10^9 solar masses for PMN J0948+0022 and 2×10^8 solar masses for PKS 1502+036, how can such large black holes exist in galaxies that are thought to be spiral hosts?

evidence.quote: Recently, Calderone et al. (2013) modelling the optical/UV data of some radio-loud NLSy1s with a Shakura & Sunyaev disc spectrum estimated BH masses higher than 10^8 M⊙. In particular, they derived a BH mass of 10^9 M⊙ and 2×10^8 M⊙ for PMN J0948+0022 and PKS 1502+036, respectively, in agreement with the typical BH mass of blazars.

This may solve the problem of the minimum BH mass predicted in different scenarios of relativistic jet formation and development, but introduces a new issue. If the BH mass of these NLSy1s is 10^8-10^9 M⊙, how is it possible to have such a large BH mass in a spiral galaxy?

Considering also that NLSy1s are thought to be hosted in spiral galaxies, their detection in γ rays poses intriguing questions about the nature of these sources, the production of relativistic jets, the mechanisms of high-energy emission, and the cosmological evolution of radio-loud AGN.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are a class of active galactic nuclei traditionally believed to host central supermassive black holes of relatively low mass (∼10^6–10^8 solar masses) in spiral host galaxies, and to accrete near or above the Eddington limit. Standard accretion-disc modeling (e.g., fitting the optical/UV continuum with a Shakura–Sunyaev thin-disc spectrum) of certain radio-loud, γ-ray–emitting NLSy1s yields central black-hole mass estimates as large as 10^8–10^9 solar masses; in particular, such modeling gives M_BH ≈ 10^9 M_⊙ for PMN J0948+0022 and M_BH ≈ 2×10^8 M_⊙ for PKS 1502+036, comparable to typical blazar black-hole masses.

Within standard models of galaxy–black hole co-evolution, black holes of mass 10^8–10^9 M_⊙ are expected to reside in massive elliptical hosts rather than in spiral galaxies, since spiral bulges generally cannot accommodate such masses via the M_BH–σ and M_BH–M_bulge scaling relations.

Problem. Provide a physically consistent explanation for how supermassive black holes of mass 10^8–10^9 M_⊙ can exist in spiral host galaxies, as appears to be required by the corrected mass estimates for radio-loud γ-ray–emitting NLSy1 galaxies. In particular, reconcile the inferred large black-hole masses with (i) the established M_BH–bulge scaling relations, (ii) the morphological classification of these systems as disc/spiral hosts, and (iii) standard pictures of relativistic-jet formation that traditionally tie powerful jets to elliptical hosts with massive black holes.
artifact.category_tag: Active galactic nuclei and supermassive black holes
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent host-galaxy imaging and modeling studies of γ-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1s suggest the issue is partially resolved: several γ-NLSy1 hosts have been confirmed to have disc/spiral-like morphologies, indicating that powerful relativistic jets and high black-hole masses are not exclusive to elliptical hosts and that the classical "jet paradigm" may not hold. However, the question of whether 10^8–10^9 M_⊙ black holes can self-consistently coexist with spiral hosts (and whether some apparent spirals are in fact merger remnants or pseudo-bulge systems) remains an active area of investigation, with ongoing host-imaging campaigns and revised black-hole mass estimates still being debated.

status_evidence.title: Jetted narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies breaking the jet paradigm: A comprehensive study of host-galaxy morphologies
status_evidence.snippet: Most γ-NLSy1 sources show disk-like host morphologies, supporting the view that the launching of relativistic jets is independent of host galaxy type.
status_evidence.claim: Recent host-galaxy imaging supports the existence of jetted NLSy1s with high black-hole masses in disc/spiral-type hosts, indicating the elliptical-only jet paradigm is not strictly required.

status_evidence.title: Are Narrow-line Seyfert 1 Galaxies Powered by Low-mass Black Holes?
status_evidence.snippet: Re-examination of black-hole mass estimates suggests NLSy1s may host more massive black holes than traditionally inferred.
status_evidence.claim: There is ongoing debate and revision regarding NLSy1 black-hole masses, with some methods yielding higher values consistent with 10^8–10^9 M_⊙.

status_evidence.title: Near-infrared morphologies of the host galaxies of narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies
status_evidence.snippet: Near-IR imaging of NLSy1 hosts reveals a mix of disc-dominated and bulge/merger-related morphologies.
status_evidence.claim: Host morphology studies suggest a more nuanced picture, partially addressing how massive black holes can reside in apparently spiral hosts.
